title: Modulus, arguments, and polar geometry
terms: modulus; absolute value; argument; principal argument; polar form; triangle inequality in C.

exposition.text:

2 2
For z = x + iy, its modulus is |z| = x + y . For z ̸= 0, write z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) with
r = |z| > 0. Arguments differ by multiples of 2π; the principal argument convention here is
−π < Arg z ≤ π. Zero has modulus zero but has no argument. Products multiply moduli and
add arguments, with adjustment back to the principal interval when needed.
The identity |z − w| equals Euclidean distance makes complex equations into geometric loci. In
particular, equal distances give a perpendicular bisector, and a nonunit ratio of distances gives
an Apollonius circle. The inequalities ||z|−|w|| ≤ |z +w| ≤ |z|+|w| are useful without computing
coordinates.

question.text:
Which set is described by |z| + |z − 2| = 2?
(A) The circle |z − 1| = 1.
(B) The closed real segment [0, 2].
(C) The two points 0 and 2 only.
(D) The whole real axis.
(E) The disk |z − 1| ≤ 1.

solution.text:
The triangle inequality gives |z| + |2 − z| ≥ 2. Equality requires the two vectors z and
2 − z to point in the same direction, allowing a zero vector. Since they sum to the positive
real number two, both must be nonnegative real. Thus precisely 0 ≤ z ≤ 2 works. This is
the degenerate ellipse case.

question.text:

(A) 5/3 (B) −5/3 (C) −1 (D) 1/3 (E) 0

solution.text:

Writing z = x + iy and squaring gives (x − 1) + y = 4((x + 1) + y ). This simplifies to
2 2
(x + 5/3) + y = 16/9, a circle centered at the real point −5/3.

For z ̸= 0, suppose arg z = π/5 modulo 2π. What is the principal argument of −z , in (−π, π]?
(A) 4π/5 (B) −3π/5 (C) 2π/5 (D) 3π/5 (E) −2π/5

solution.text:
Conjugation negates the argument, cubing multiplies it by three, and multiplication by −1
adds π. Thus the resulting argument is −3π/5 + π = 2π/5, already in the principal range.
